candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Weighted stochastic decision processes may still fail to provide the unrestricted authorship that incompatibilists associate with free will.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly adopts an incompatibilist perspective hypothetically and develops objections to weighted stochastic choice.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly tests whether probabilistic alternatives improve on randomness enough to satisfy libertarian freedom and responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The earlier claim that constrained neural indeterminacy avoids the determined-or-random dilemma.

candidates.contextSummary: After Hawkins describes evolutionary variation and executive selection in the brain, Folley reconstructs how an incompatibilist might challenge probabilistically weighted choice.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: If the self is identified with the brain's executive or valitional system, that self participates in setting the criteria governing indeterminate choice.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly answers the preceding probabilistic objection by asking what the choosing self could be and locating it in executive brain function.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Hawkins's sourcehood answer by identifying the agent with the system that imposes constraints on indeterminate neural activity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's reconstruction of the incompatibilist demand for choice beyond a preset probability distribution.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins responds to the demand that the person, rather than probabilities, must choose by locating the person in the valitional system applying selection criteria.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Libertarian sourcehood need not require a detached soul because either agent causation or the conscious valitional brain can initiate the relevant action.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker identifies a libertarian agent-causal account and then connects it to the previously described neuroscientific role of conscious valitional processes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move offers two accounts of agent sourcehood and argues that the neuroscientific model can meet the demand for a genuine initiating agent.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The suggestion that incompatibilists reject only a magical self hovering above physical processes.

candidates.contextSummary: Following discussion of whether traditional incompatibilism assumes a dualist will, Hawkins distinguishes agent causation from his preferred brain-based account of sourcehood.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: A person's evaluative criteria are heavily constrained by genetics and upbringing, leaving much of the space of possible choices outside that person's control.
candidates.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly presents the other incompatibilist line and closes by asking Hawkins how his libertarian account responds to it.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection targets ultimate sourcehood by shifting attention from indeterminate selection to the externally formed criteria that structure selection.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins's claim that the conscious valitional brain supplies the sourcehood incompatibilists request.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley grants the possible role of neural indeterminacy but argues that inherited and environmental factors still determine or restrict the criteria governing choice.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Libertarian freedom can operate within biological and social limits because agents contribute through repeated choices to their own long-term self-realization.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins expressly accepts limits on libertarian freedom and develops a positive account of constrained choice reshaping later character and possibilities.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response explains how meaningful agency and self-formation remain possible even when biology, society, and environment substantially constrain initial options.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's objection that genetics and upbringing externally determine the criteria constraining later choices.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins concedes extensive external influence, then uses cumulative decisions and learning as examples of agents changing their brains and expanding future options.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: An idealist but non-dualist metaphysics makes subjective deliberation fundamental and predicts a physical correlate of experienced choosing in the brain.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins identifies his own idealist and non-dualist commitments and explains how they relate subjective volition to observable neural processes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move grounds his neuroscientific libertarian account in a broader metaphysics and defends taking first-person deliberative experience seriously.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The question whether Hawkins's libertarianism rests on broader philosophy or merely an intuition about deliberation.

candidates.contextSummary: Asked for the basis of his libertarian view, Hawkins explains that idealism treats physical brain activity as the manifestation of fundamentally mental reality.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Hawkins's limited libertarianism may deny the ultimate sourcehood and responsibility commonly sought when an agent's evaluative outlook is formed by a restrictive environment.
candidates.attributionBasis: Folley states his concern about self-causing libertarianism and develops the racist-upbringing example as a challenge to Hawkins's restricted criteria account.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The example presses whether Hawkins can preserve robust moral responsibility when an agent never had meaningful access to alternative evaluative criteria.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins's claim that constrained agents still contribute to self-realization through indeterminate, criteria-guided choices.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley contrasts popular expectations of libertarian sourcehood with Hawkins's more modest model, using a socially isolated racist agent to expose the difference.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism should reconstruct the practically important notions of freedom and will that survive determinism rather than claim that traditional libertarian freedom survives intact.
candidates.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly reframes the compatibilist project and illustrates it with a deterministic community distinguishing tumor-driven behavior from ordinary agency.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is a direct constructive statement of the compatibilist position on the motion, identifying what agency can mean if determinism is assumed true.
candidates.contextSummary: After noting the long history of compatibilist ideas, Folley argues for preserving distinctions between chosen and unchosen conduct through rational and predictive models.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Indeterminate neuronal firing combined with system-level criterial constraints supplies uncaused neural events and top-down causation without requiring neurons to emerge from nothing.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins directly answers the demand for an uncaused neuron by describing synaptic indeterminacy and system-level criterial causation in the cited model.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response addresses the physical mechanism at the heart of his libertarian view and distinguishes top-down agency from simple billiard-ball causation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's and hard incompatibilists' demand for a physically identifiable uncaused neural contribution to choice.

candidates.contextSummary: Invited to answer Folley's questions, Hawkins argues that firing can lack a sufficient determining cause while executive constraints operate downward at the system level.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Libertarian freedom requires alternatives that are genuinely live for the agent, so severe biological or social constraints can reduce freedom and moral responsibility by degree.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins distinguishes impossible or psychologically unavailable options from live alternatives and applies that distinction to responsibility for racist beliefs.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move clarifies the scope of alternative possibilities in his libertarianism and states when constrained agents lack the responsibility normally tied to freedom.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's racist-upbringing example and objection that restricted criteria undermine sourcehood and responsibility.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins accepts that biology and upbringing constrain options, but argues that freedom exists among live alternatives and responsibility diminishes when none are available.
